name: Bonnor-Vaidya Charged Radiating Star
description: Vaidya's radiating star with a charge: the field of a spherical body that sends out, or takes in, null dust carrying electric charge as well as energy, found by William Bonnor and Prahlad Vaidya in 1970 as an exact solution of the Einstein-Maxwell equations. Its mass and its charge are functions of a null time, and where both are constant it is the charged black hole of Reissner and Nordström.
convention: We work in units with $c = 1$. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Light carries energy away from a star, and Vaidya's metric follows the mass of the star as it goes [vaidya1951]. Could the light carry electric charge away too? The question came up at Queen Elizabeth College in London, where Prahlad Vaidya was visiting William Bonnor on a British Council exchange, and their answer reached the journal on 10 April 1970 [bonnor1970]. They gave solutions of the Einstein-Maxwell equations "describing the emission of charged null fluid from a spherically symmetric body" [bonnor1970]. A null fluid is a stream of light, every parcel of it moving straight out at the speed of light, and theirs carries charge along with its energy [bonnor1970]. About nature they were candid: charged null fluid "is a model for a charged photon fluid, though whether the latter exists in nature remains to be seen" [bonnor1970].¶The recipe is Vaidya's own, used twice: take the charged black hole of Reissner and Nordström and let its mass $m$ and its charge $q$ both depend on the moment at which a light ray leaves the star, so that each ray carries off a little of both [bonnor1970, ori1991charged]. The metric keeps Reissner-Nordström's $1 - 2m/r + q^2/r^2$, with $m$ and $q$ now changing from one ray to the next [ori1991charged]. Its electric field surprised them: it "varies as $r^{-2}$, and is parallel to the direction of energy propagation" [bonnor1970]. In Vaidya's earlier radiating star with a field, they noted, the field lies across the rays and falls off as $1/r$ [bonnor1970]. The line element itself was already on paper: it turns up in February 1968 in Jerzy Plebański and John Stachel's sorting of the Einstein tensors possible in spherical symmetry, two years before Bonnor and Vaidya gave it a physical reading [plebanski1968, bick2026].¶Run the film backward and the charged light falls in, onto a charged black hole or onto empty space, and there the metric misbehaves: close in, the dust has negative energy [ori1991charged]. Its energy density is proportional to $\dot m - q\dot q/r$, with the dot a derivative along the rays, so it is negative inside the radius $r_c = q\dot q/\dot m$ whenever the charge grows with the mass [ori1991charged]. From 1980 to 1991 that was taken as it stood, the dust moving on geodesics with the negative energy accepted [kehle2024]. The negative energy was even put to work: in Yasuhito Kaminaga's model of 1990 it shrinks a charged black hole away, as evaporation would [kaminaga1990, chatterjee2016]. Kayll Lake and T. Zannias let the mass and the charge grow in step with the advanced time, so that the collapse looks the same at every scale, and found that it generically ends in a naked singularity [lake1991, koh2024]. To Amos Ori it was "rather disturbing" that a model as simple as "a stream of massless charged particles" should lead to "the undesired result of negative energies" [ori1991charged].¶The earlier readings had left out the electric force [chatterjee2016]. A charge falling toward a like charge is pushed back, light or not, and Ori derived from the Einstein-Maxwell equations an equation of motion for the dust with a Lorentz force in it [ori1991charged]. Picture a ball thrown up a hill: the dust loses energy all the way in, and at $r_c$ its energy "has been reduced to zero" [ori1991charged]. There it turns round and leaves along an outgoing ray, gaining energy as it goes [ori1991charged]. Where the turning surface is spacelike, the spacetime to its future is a piece of Bonnor and Vaidya's outgoing metric, and "charged null fluid always satisfies the weak energy condition" [ori1991charged].¶Can a charged black hole be fed until its two horizons merge and its surface gravity drops to zero, all in a finite time? Werner Israel's third law of black hole mechanics of 1986 says no, provided the infalling matter has a bounded energy tensor and positive energy near the apparent horizon [israel1986]. He and B. T. Sullivan had tried it on this dust in 1980 and found the extreme state within reach only where the dust has negative energy [sullivan1980, kehle2022]. With Ori's bounce the energy is positive everywhere, and the hole gets there all the same: Christoph Kehle and Ryan Unger built bouncing dust in 2024 in which "a subextremal Reissner-Nordström apparent horizon can evolve into an extremal Reissner-Nordström event horizon in finite advanced time" [kehle2024]. Their first counterexample to the third law, of 2022, uses a charged scalar field that starts from regular initial data [kehle2022].¶With the charge held fixed and only the mass varying, the same metric plays "a very important role" in Eric Poisson and Israel's mass inflation, the unbounded growth of the mass function at the inner horizon of a charged black hole [poisson1990, chatterjee2016]. Ori's bounce left one case open: where the turning surface is timelike the dust going in crosses the dust coming out, and for that "as yet the analytic form of such a solution is unknown" [ori1991charged]. By 2016 the bounce had been carried to higher dimensions and to anti-de Sitter space, by Soumyabrata Chatterjee, Suman Ganguli, and Amitabh Virmani [chatterjee2016]. The timelike case was reached in 2026, when David Bick showed that any timelike curve segment in the plane of time and radius of Minkowski or Reissner-Nordström spacetime is the bounce of some beam of charged null dust sent in from past null infinity [bick2026]. Kehle and Unger list what is still wrong with the dust: its density is unbounded along the bounce, and there its equations do not fix the future from initial data [kehle2024].

related.text: The same star with no charge to shed. With $q = 0$ the metric is Vaidya's [vaidya1951].
The charged black hole that neither gains nor loses. With $m$ and $q$ constant the metric is Reissner-Nordström's in Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates, with $r_s = 2m$ and $r_q = q$ [ori1991charged].
No charge and a constant mass. The metric is then Schwarzschild's in Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates, with $r_s = 2m$.

coordinates.name: Outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein
domains: r\,\partial_u m = q\,\partial_u q \;\text{(where the energy density of the null dust changes sign)}

parameters.description: Mass inside the sphere of radius $r$ at the retarded time $u$, a length, $m = GM/c^2$
Charge inside that sphere, a length, $q^2 = GQ^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4)$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the retarded time $u$ a length and $r$ the areal radius. The mass $m(u)$ and the charge $q(u)$ are functions of $u$ alone, both lengths. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
geodesics: \ddot{r} - \dfrac{r^4\,\partial_u m - q\,r^3\,\partial_u q - \left(m\,r - q^2\right)\left(r^2 - 2m\,r + q^2\right)}{r^5}\dot{u}^2 + \dfrac{2m\,r - 2q^2}{r^3}\dot{u}\dot{r} - \dfrac{r^2 - 2m\,r + q^2}{r}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{\left(r^2 - 2m\,r + q^2\right)\sin^2\theta}{r}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein
domains: r\,\partial_v m = q\,\partial_v q \;\text{(where the energy density of the null dust changes sign)}

parameters.description: Mass inside the sphere of radius $r$ at the advanced time $v$, a length, $m = GM/c^2$
Charge inside that sphere, a length, $q^2 = GQ^2/(4\pi\epsilon_0c^4)$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the advanced time $v$ a length and $r$ the areal radius. The mass $m(v)$ and the charge $q(v)$ are functions of $v$ alone, both lengths. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
geodesics: \ddot{r} + \dfrac{r^4\,\partial_v m - q\,r^3\,\partial_v q + \left(m\,r - q^2\right)\left(r^2 - 2m\,r + q^2\right)}{r^5}\dot{v}^2 - \dfrac{2m\,r - 2q^2}{r^3}\dot{v}\dot{r} - \dfrac{r^2 - 2m\,r + q^2}{r}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{\left(r^2 - 2m\,r + q^2\right)\sin^2\theta}{r}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Homothetic
domains: V \to -\infty \;\text{(the first ray, }v = 0\text{, flat space before it)}
2\mu R^3 - MR^2 + 2M^2R - MQ^2 = 0 \;\text{(the rays that keep their }R\text{)}
R = Q^2/M \;\text{(where the energy density of the null dust changes sign)}

parameters.description: Mass scale, a length: the mass is $m = Me^{\mu V/M}$, which grows as $\mu v$ in the advanced time $v = (M/\mu)e^{\mu V/M}$
Charge scale, a length: the charge is $q = Qe^{\mu V/M}$, in proportion to the mass
Rate $dm/dv$ at which the mass grows, a pure number

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(V, R, \theta, \phi)$, both lengths, for the mass and the charge that grow in proportion to the advanced time $v$: $V$ is its logarithm, $v = (M/\mu)e^{\mu V/M}$, and $R = rM/m$ is the areal radius $r$ in units of the mass $m = \mu v$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
geodesics: \ddot{R} - \dfrac{\left(M\,R - Q^2\right)\left(2\mu\,R^3 - M\,R^2 + 2M^2\,R - M\,Q^2\right)}{M\,R^5}\dot{V}^2 + \dfrac{2\mu\,R^3 - 2M^2\,R + 2M\,Q^2}{M\,R^3}\dot{V}\dot{R} + \dfrac{\mu\,R^3 - M\,R^2 + 2M^2\,R - M\,Q^2}{M\,R}\dot{\theta}^2 + \dfrac{\left(\mu\,R^3 - M\,R^2 + 2M^2\,R - M\,Q^2\right)\sin^2\theta}{M\,R}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0
